title: Queueing sandwich effect and collective saturation journal
content:
Summary:

This is a working log of an empirical phenomenon we've repeatedly seen during multi-GPU collective-heavy LLM inference: bursts that start on the host or requester path propagate through PCIe staging, NVLink/ARB aggregation, and finally into GPU ingress queues in a stacked manner, producing disproportionate tail latency spikes for collective ops (all-reduce/all-gather). We are calling the end-to-end effect the 'queueing sandwich' because high occupancy layers surround a thin fast-path and the transition timing creates backpressure and jitter.

Experiment goals:
- Reproduce a minimal workload that exposes sandwich-shaped queue buildup across host <-> GPU links.
- Measure where latency mass accumulates (host CPU xmit, PCIe write stalls, NVLink hop queues, GPU SM scheduling).
- Quantify sensitivity to collective fanout degree, chunk size, and small-packet interleaving.
- Evaluate mitigations: pacing, staggered start, prefill heuristics, and adaptive fanout.

Testbed & configuration notes:
- HW: 8x A100-esque accelerators per node, dual-socket host (2x 24C), Mellanox HDR interconnect between nodes for cross-node multi-GPU tests.
- Topology: multiple racks examined; primary notes here from same-rack, single-host multi-GPU config using NVLink mesh (full mesh) with PCIe Gen4 x16 host links.
- SW: linux 6.1 kernel, NCCL 2.18 experimental, runtime branch: feature/comm-observability (PR 1124).
- Workloads: synthetic all-reduce micro-bench (n=512 floats per GPU per round), LLM token decode traces (batch-size 1–8, seq-len 32–1024), and a simulated KV-cache fill/prefill microbenchmark that does a pattern of prefix traffic followed by large KV transfers.
- Instrumentation: perf counters (PCIe Tx/Rx stalls), nvprof-like NVTX ranges, NCCLTRACE logging, eBPF for application->kernel queue times, GPU SM queue depth via driver counters, and host NIC transmit ring metrics via ethtool/pmcq.

Key observations (empirical):
1) Two-layer accumulation: In the worst runs the majority of extra latency appears first as increases in host kernel TX queue wait times (up to tens of ms), then as PCIe write backlog (measured by increasing DMA descriptor pending counts), and finally as NVLink TX arbitration delays that cause packets to be delivered in bursts to GPU ingress queues. The visible symptom at the application layer is one or two 10–50 ms long spikes per collective call in an otherwise 1–3 ms median.

2) Collective fanout interacts nonlinearly with sandwich formation: Medium-sized fanouts (4–6 peers) caused higher tail mass than maximum fanout (all peers) in some topologies. Hypothesis: partial fanout creates partial aggregation points that produce intermediate queuing hotspots, whereas full fanout distributes load evenly across all endpoints.

3) Small-chunk interleaving worsens tail: When chunk size < 8KB we observe more frequent microbursts — many small DMA descriptors get queued and serialized through the PCIe/NVLink pipeline, creating packetization overheads and more arbitration events on NVLink. Larger chunk sizes (>=64KB) reduce the number of arbitration cycles and lower tail-latency at the cost of slightly higher median transfer time.

4) Prefill heuristic helps but needs tuning: Prefilling GPU KV-cache lanes before burst phases reduces spike count but increases baseline occupancy which can hurt hot-path latency for latency-sensitive single-token decodes. Prefill should be gated by a dynamic SLO-aware threshold.

Profiling excerpts (high-level):
- Host TX queue time: median 0.6 ms, p99 47.3 ms (worst-case run).
- PCIe DMA pending descriptors: median 8 descriptors, p99 198 descriptors.
- NVLink arbitration delay per-packet: median 12 us, p99 2.1 ms in saturated bursts.
- NCCL collectives: all-reduce latency median 2.4 ms, p99 58.6 ms (matches host tx queue spikes).

Reproduction steps (short):
1) Checkout branch feature/comm-observability, enable NCCLTRACE and nvtx ranges.
2) Run synthetic-rdma-collective --peers=6 --chunk=4k --rounds=300 --interarrival=0 (tight loop).
3) Collect host eBPF trace (trace tcp/rdma submit paths), nvprof NVTX ranges, and driver counters.
4) Inspect host tx queue histograms and correlate with NCCL trace timestamps.

Attempted mitigations & results:
- Tight pacing at application level (sleep microseconds between submits): reduces p99 by ~30% but increases median by ~10% and hurts throughput. Good as emergency mitigation.
- Staggered start across replicas (add jitter in start time): reduces synchronous stacking of DMA submits and drops p99 by ~45% in multi-host runs.
- Chunk-size upshifts (4KB -> 64KB): reduces per-call arbitration overhead and lowers both median and tail for collectives involving more than 4 peers. Tradeoff: slightly larger memory copies.
- NIC offload tuning (tx queue mapping): mapping NIC TX queues to fewer cores reduced host-side serialization in our testbed; however not portable across customer kernels.
- NCCL-level fanout tuning (limit-degree): setting a topology-aware degree cap to avoid creating intermediate aggregation hotspots produced the best balance (median unchanged, p99 improved ~55%).

Open questions & next experiments:
- Can we detect in real time the sandwich buildup using only host-visible metrics? Candidates: sustained growth in host tx queue time + rising PCIe pending descriptors + sudden NVLink arbitration latency spikes. Need a simple classifier (maybe a two-feature threshold) that can trigger fallback routing.
- How does CPU core scheduling affect the sandwich? We saw correlation between submit CPU hop and increased host tx times; a controlled test with pinned clients is next.
- Cross-node variant: does RDMA/NIC buffering create a third significant layer that changes optimal fanout? Initial cross-node runs show RDMA NIC ingress queues add another staging layer and can invert the medium-fanout penalty.
- Does QUIC-like pacing at the transport level (rate buckets) help more than ad-hoc application pacing? Implementation experiment planned (INF-3842).

Immediate recommendations for serving runtime:
- Add a light-weight sandwich detector that monitors: host_tx_queue_p50/p90/p99, pci_pending_descs, and nvlink_arbit_ms_p90. Use a rolling 10s window and generate a signal if all three rise beyond empirical thresholds.
- Implement topology-aware degree limits in NCCL orchestration layer: if sandwich detector fires, reduce degree for newly-scheduled collectives and prefer broader full-fanout or pairwise pipeline rather than partial-tree fanouts.
- Expose chunk-size tuning knob per-model in runtime config with safe defaults (start at 32KB for medium shard sizes).
- Add a prefill mode that is SLO-aware: only prefill when the predicted token latency budget > X ms (experiment to find X).

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Run pinned-core isolation experiments (no hyperthreading) and collect host queue metrics (assigned to Priya).
- Implement simple sandwich-detector prototype in feature/comm-observability (Noah).
- Schedule cross-node NIC ingress experiment (Jordan + infra).
- Draft RFC for topology-aware fanout policy and include examples for Dedicated customers (Draft due 2024-12-05).

Attachments & logs:
- raw-traces/2024-11-10-run3-nccltrace.log (attached in folder)
- perf-counter-dumps/2024-11-10-pcie-descriptors.csv
- flamegraphs/2024-11-10-host-submit.svg (see drive folder)

Closing thought:
This 'sandwich' framing helped the team reason about stacked buffering layers and why some middle-ground strategies (e.g., partial fanout) can paradoxically hurt tail latency. The next phase is to convert the detector idea into a runtime autopolicy that can toggle fanout and chunking on-the-fly depending on observed signals — the aim is graceful degradation rather than wholesale throttling.

Unresolved: quantitative thresholds for detector (need more runs across rack topologies).

End of journal entry.
